item.title: Sounkyo Gorge & Onsen — Guide
item.description: Sounkyo, on the northeastern edge of Daisetsuzan National Park in central Hokkaido, is a spectacular gorge combined with a hot-spring (onsen) resort town, making it one of the region’s most popular natural destinations. The gorge stretches for around 24 km along the Ishikari River, walled by dramatic columnar cliffs of volcanic rock rising sheer above the valley. Its most famous sights are two beautiful waterfalls that plunge down the cliff faces — Ryusei (‘Shooting Star’) Falls and Ginga (‘Milky Way’) Falls, best viewed together from a nearby lookout.

item.title: Daisetsuzan National Park Guide: Hiking, Ropeway & Autumn
item.description: Daisetsuzan is the vast, wild roof of Hokkaido — the island’s largest national park, sometimes called “the playground of the gods” by the Ainu. A sprawling massif of volcanic peaks, alpine meadows, gorges and hot springs, it centres on Asahidake, Hokkaido’s highest mountain (2,291 m). A ropeway whisks visitors into the high country for easy boardwalk strolls or serious hikes, and each September the park lights up with Japan’s earliest autumn colours.

item.title: Hokkaido Autumn Foliage Guide: Best Spots & Time (Sep–Oct)
item.description: Autumn comes first to Hokkaido — Japan’s earliest foliage flames into life on the high peaks in September, weeks ahead of the mainland, before sweeping down to the lakes, valleys and city parks through October. The island’s huge wild landscapes make for spectacular koyo: golden birch and larch, crimson maples and mountain ash against volcanic peaks and mirror-still caldera lakes. From the alpine slopes of Daisetsuzan to the gorges of Sounkyo and the onsen valley of Jozankei, Hokkaido’s autumn is a quieter, wilder counterpoint to Kyoto’s crowds.

item.title: Hokkaido Nature Guide: Shiretoko, Daisetsuzan, Furano & Kushiro
item.description: Hokkaido’s nature operates on a scale that Japan’s other islands cannot match. The island is 83,000 square kilometres — roughly the size of Austria — and contains 6 national parks, including Japan’s largest (Daisetsuzan) and one of its two UNESCO World Heritage natural sites (Shiretoko). The wildlife is genuinely wild: brown bears that fish for salmon in rivers accessible from the road, red-crowned cranes that are among the world’s rarest birds, and an autumn foliage season that begins 3–4 weeks before the rest of Japan.
